title: Faith like a mustard seed (Luke 17:1–10)
hookLine: the apostles ask for more faith; he says a mustard seed is enough

cards: I need more. More faith, more certainty. If I just believed harder, I could do the hard thing.
Some people of faith know that request well, and Luke shows exactly when the apostles make it. Not after a storm or a miracle.
Right after Jesus gives them an instruction about forgiveness that sounds, frankly, impossible. Their reply is three words in the King James Bible, with nothing polished about it.

teach.b: Here's the instruction: if your brother wrongs you, tell him; if he repents, forgive him.

"And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him." Anyone who's lived with a sibling or a roommate knows how hard that is.
So the apostles say: "Increase our faith." And Jesus doesn't.

He answers: "If ye had faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye might say unto this sycamine tree, Be thou plucked up by the root, and be thou planted in the sea; and it should obey you." A mustard seed is tiny.
A sycamine is a full-grown tree. Uprooting it and planting it in the sea is a deliberately absurd picture. Readers hear this in more than one way.

Some hear a gentle rebuke: you don't yet have even a seed's worth. Others hear encouragement: even a speck of real trust in God is enough to do impossible things, so you don't need more before you start.
Then a short story that sounds harsh at first. A servant comes in from plowing, and his master doesn't say, sit down, let me serve you. The servant makes dinner first.
So you too, Jesus says, when you've done everything you were told, say: "We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do."
On that reading, forgiving seven times a day isn't a heroic feat that needs a giant supply of faith.
It's the next job, done with a little faith. No medal.

teach.h: IF YE HAD FAITH AS A GRAIN OF MUSTARD SEED.
teach.b: Just the work, and the seed doing what seeds do.

how: Some Christians pray the apostles' words, increase our faith, in times of doubt, and some churches teach that faith grows by acting on it in small daily obedience rather than waiting for certainty.

o: a big harvest, the reward for strong faith
a tiny seed, a speck of faith that can move a tree
a bitter herb eaten to remember slavery

games.q: what's inside Luke 17:1–10 — tap the pairs.

s: the apostles ask for more faith just after hearing about forgiving seven times a day
an impossible-sounding instruction, then: "increase our faith."
Jesus tells them they need much more faith
he says faith as small as a mustard seed is enough.
Jesus says a servant should be thanked for doing what he was told
"we have done that which was our duty to do."

games.q: Jesus tells you: if someone wrongs you seven times in a day and says I repent seven times, forgive them. what do you say?
games.why: the apostles say "increase our faith." Jesus says a mustard seed's worth is enough to uproot a sycamine tree.

practice: Think of something you've been putting off until you feel more ready, an apology, a forgiveness, a step in prayer, and notice the voice that says not yet.
Picture a mustard seed, small enough to lose in your palm, and name the smallest first step you could take with what you've got. If you pray, say the apostles' words: increase our faith.

wordCard.voice: Mustard seed: the tiny seed Jesus names when the apostles ask for more faith, a speck that could uproot a tree.

orig.note: Greek: add! the apostles' request: add to us faith.

carryVoice: Your line: increase our faith. An honest prayer, three words long. Day five hundred sixty-two, done.
